checks.them: Okay, let's move on to some Android fundamentals. What happens when a child coroutine fails? When do you use SupervisorJob?

card.problem: What happens when a child coroutine fails, and when do you use SupervisorJob?
card.heard: child coroutine fails, when to use SupervisorJob
card.say: When a child coroutine fails, it cancels its parent. The parent then cancels all its other children, and the failure goes up to the scope. So one failed request can kill unrelated work in the same scope. I use SupervisorJob when the children should fail independently, like separate requests on one screen. One failure then doesn't cancel the others.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

checks.them: StateFlow, SharedFlow, Channel: which one for one-time UI events?

card.problem: StateFlow, SharedFlow or Channel for one-time UI events?
card.heard: StateFlow, SharedFlow, Channel for one-time UI events
card.say: For one-time UI events, I'd use a Channel. A StateFlow always keeps the latest value, so a new collector gets an old event again. A SharedFlow with no replay can drop an event when nobody is collecting. A Channel delivers each event once, to one collector. I'd receive it with `receiveAsFlow` and collect it with `repeatOnLifecycle`, so events aren't lost when the screen is in the background.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

I'd receive it with `receiveAsFlow` and collect it with `repeatOnLifecycle`, so events aren't lost when the screen is in the background.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

results.detail: PASS: The answer compares all three correctly — StateFlow replays the latest value to new collectors, a no-replay SharedFlow can drop events with no collector, and a Channel delivers each event once to one collector — and picks Channel with a clear reason, in short spoken form.

checks.them: Why do we use repeatOnLifecycle to collect a Flow?

card.problem: StateFlow, SharedFlow or Channel for one-time UI events?
card.heard: Why use repeatOnLifecycle to collect a Flow?
card.say: It ties collection to the screen's lifecycle. When the screen goes to the background, collection stops, so we don't keep doing work nobody sees. When it comes back, collection starts again, so the UI always gets fresh data. Without it, a collector on the Activity keeps running and can leak or crash.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

checks.them: Let's switch gears to some live coding. Write a function that takes a Flow of String of SSE text chunks and emits complete events. A chunk can cut an event anywhere.

card.problem: Write a function that takes a Flow of String SSE chunks and emits complete events
card.heard: live coding — Flow of SSE chunks to complete events
card.say: Okay, I'll write a function that takes the chunk flow and returns a flow of complete events. I'll keep a buffer for the partial text, split on the blank line between events, and emit only the parts that are complete.
card.type: add@parseSseEvents: fun parseSseEvents(chunks: Flow<String>): Flow<String> = flow { ⏎     val buffer = StringBuilder() ⏎     chunks.collect { chunk -> ⏎         buffer.append(chunk) ⏎         while (true) { ⏎             val end = buffer.indexOf("\n\n") ⏎             if (end == -1) break ⏎             val event = buffer.substring(0, end) ⏎             buffer.delete(0, end + 2) ⏎             emit(event) ⏎         } ⏎     } ⏎ }
card.then: Next I'd handle the leftover buffer at the end of the stream, and the case where a chunk splits the "\n\n" itself.

card.problem: Design the Android client for a ChatGPT-like app: streaming chat, stop/regenerate, photo upload, voice mode, history synced across phone and web; define what the client needs from the backend
card.adopted: Room is the single source of truth; the Repository is the only writer, the ViewModel reads from Room, and the UI observes the ViewModel
card.constraints: ["Client needs a stable answer id and a sequence number on stream pieces for stop, regenerate and ordering"]
card.heard: draw the main layers, where the data lives
card.say: I'd keep the layers simple. The Chat screen observes the ViewModel, and the ViewModel only reads from Room. The Repository is the only writer: it sends the request, reads the stream, and saves each piece into Room. So Room is the single source of truth, and the UI never talks to the network directly. History syncs by pulling the server's message list and merging it into Room.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, thanks for joining. I'm one of the Android engineers here. Let's start easy: tell me about yourself in two minutes.
Candidate: Good morning, I'm Jianhui.
Candidate: I have ten years of experience in software development, mainly working on Android apps.
Candidate: Over the past three years, I've also been working on AI products, from development to launch.
Candidate: My most recent job was at KKday, a travel platform in Asia.
Candidate: I worked on the main features of the Android app and made the app run faster.
Candidate: For example, I fixed the lag when users switched between product options.
Candidate: At the same time, I was the technical lead for an AI trip planning project.
Candidate: I was responsible for the technical plan, the agent architecture, and the main backend development.
Candidate: With this feature, users could plan their trips with AI directly in the app.
Candidate: After we launched it, the system handled about 300,000 trip planning requests every day.
Candidate: Before KKday, I worked at Kezhi Technology, an AI education startup.
Candidate: I was the only Android engineer there.
Candidate: I built the Android app and worked with my team to launch the first version in just four weeks.
Candidate: That's also when I started working on AI features myself.
Candidate: I built the whole Android app myself, from zero to launch.
Candidate: Before that, I worked on Android apps at Debon Securities, and I also spent six years on Android apps at Ping An.
Candidate: I'm interested in ActAI because you're bringing AI into everyday communication.
Candidate: I also have my own app, Cabinet AI, which explores when AI should act on its own and when it should ask first.
Interviewer: What did you build most recently on Android?
Candidate: The most recent Android work is the Android version of Cabinet AI.
Candidate: I wrote it in Kotlin and Compose, and I built the base framework myself.
Candidate: I used AI coding tools for the simple screens, and it isn't on Google Play yet.
Interviewer: Walk me through the SSE itinerary feature at KKday, from server to screen.
Candidate: Sure.
Candidate: The user sends a destination, a budget and a number of days.
Candidate: The backend agent picks places and bookable products, then streams the plan back as SSE events, one day at a time.
Candidate: On Android, I read that stream and show each day card as it arrives, so Day 1 appears while the rest is still being made.

Candidate: If the connection drops mid-stream, I resume from the last fully received day rather than restarting, and I cap retries so a persistent failure surfaces as an error instead of looping silently.
Interviewer: What exactly did you write on Android, and what did your team write?
Candidate: On Android, I wrote the SSE client myself.
Candidate: That means the stream reading, the day card list, and the resume and retry logic.
Candidate: I also wrote the code that checks each card before it shows.
Candidate: The backend agent, the product tools and the personalization data layer were my design, but the backend team wrote most of that code.
Candidate: The app team built the screens around my cards.
Interviewer: The crash rate went down 90% at Debon. What was the hardest crash?
Candidate: The hardest one was a WebView crash on certain phone models.
Candidate: It only happened on a few devices, so it was hard to reproduce.
Candidate: I got the model list from Bugly and found a pattern.
Candidate: Then I fixed it group by group, starting with the most common one.
Candidate: Most of our crashes were null pointers, out-of-memory errors and WebView problems.
Interviewer: Tell me about a device-specific bug. How did you find it?
Candidate: At Debon, one crash only happened on a few old phone models.
Candidate: I couldn't reproduce it on my own phone.
Candidate: So I grouped the crashes by phone model in Bugly.
Candidate: The pattern showed it was an old WebView version.
Candidate: I added a version check, a simpler page for those phones, and a fallback.
Interviewer: Okay, let's move on to some Android fundamentals. What happens when a child coroutine fails? When do you use SupervisorJob?
Candidate: When a child coroutine fails, it cancels its parent.
Candidate: The parent then cancels all its other children, and the failure goes up to the scope.
Candidate: So one failed request can kill unrelated work in the same scope.
Candidate: I use SupervisorJob when the children should fail independently, like separate requests on one screen.
Candidate: One failure then doesn't cancel the others.
Interviewer: StateFlow, SharedFlow, Channel: which one for one-time UI events?
Candidate: For one-time UI events, I'd use a Channel.
Candidate: A StateFlow always keeps the latest value, so a new collector gets an old event again.
Candidate: A SharedFlow with no replay can drop an event when nobody is collecting.
Candidate: A Channel delivers each event once, to one collector.
Candidate: I'd receive it with `receiveAsFlow` and collect it with `repeatOnLifecycle`, so events aren't lost when the screen is in the background.
Interviewer: Why do we use repeatOnLifecycle to collect a Flow?
Candidate: It ties collection to the screen's lifecycle.
Candidate: When the screen goes to the background, collection stops, so we don't keep doing work nobody sees.
Candidate: When it comes back, collection starts again, so the UI always gets fresh data.
Candidate: Without it, a collector on the Activity keeps running and can leak or crash.
Interviewer: What survives process death? How do you restore the screen?
Candidate: Only saved state survives.
Candidate: I'd keep the screen's input in `SavedStateHandle`, so the ViewModel gets it back after the process is killed.
Candidate: The list of day cards I'd reload from the server, or from a local cache if we had one.
Candidate: Then the screen rebuilds from that state instead of starting empty.
Interviewer: Let's switch gears to some live coding. Write a function that takes a Flow of String of SSE text chunks and emits complete events. A chunk can cut an event anywhere.
Candidate: Okay, I'll write a function that takes the chunk flow and returns a flow of complete events.
Candidate: I'll keep a buffer for the partial text, split on the blank line between events, and emit only the parts that are complete.

[board] fun parseSseEvents(chunks: Flow<String>): Flow<String> = flow { |     val buffer = StringBuilder() |     chunks.collect { chunk -> |         buffer.append(chunk) |         while (true) { |             val end = buffer.indexOf(" |  | ") |             if (end == -1) break |             val event = buffer.substring(0, end) |             buffer.delete(0, end + 2) |             emit(event) |         } |     } |     if (buffer.isNotEmpty()) emit(buffer.toString()) | }.flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
Candidate: A chunk can split the blank line itself, so the buffer has to keep the leftover text until the next chunk arrives.

Interviewer: How do you test it?
Candidate: I'd test it at three levels.
Candidate: First, unit tests with fake chunks: one event in one chunk, one event split across two chunks, and the blank line itself split.
Candidate: Second, a chunk with two events plus a partial third.
Candidate: Third, the end of the stream, where I check the leftover is flushed once and not twice.
Candidate: I'd also run it on `Dispatchers.Default` to confirm the order stays the same.
Interviewer: What if the server sends an event with no newline at the end?
Candidate: Right now the leftover buffer is flushed at the end, so that event is emitted.
Candidate: But I'd check one thing: if the stream is cancelled, the flush never runs.
Candidate: So I'd only flush on normal completion, and drop the partial event on cancel.

Interviewer: Great. For the rest of the time, a new problem: design the Android app for ChatGPT. Users chat with the AI and see answers stream in. They can stop or regenerate an answer, upload a photo, use voice mode, and see their history on phone and web. Focus on the client. Tell me what you need from the backend.
Candidate: Before I design, let me confirm the scope.
Candidate: The client covers chat with streaming answers, stop and regenerate, photo upload, voice mode, and history synced across phone and web.
Candidate: I'll focus on the Android client and the API contract with the backend.
Candidate: Out of scope for now: model training and the web client itself.
Interviewer: Let's keep text chat, streaming, stop and history as the core. Photo and voice come later. Draw the main layers of the app. Where does the data live?
Candidate: I'd keep the layers simple.
Candidate: The Chat screen observes the ViewModel, and the ViewModel only reads from Room.
Candidate: The Repository is the only writer: it sends the request, reads the stream, and saves each piece into Room.
Candidate: So Room is the single source of truth, and the UI never talks to the network directly.
Candidate: History syncs by pulling the server's message list and merging it into Room.

Interviewer: What is your single source of truth?
Candidate: Room is the single source of truth.
Candidate: The Repository is the only writer, and it saves each streamed piece into Room as it arrives.
Candidate: The ViewModel only reads from Room, and the Chat screen observes the ViewModel.
Candidate: So the UI never talks to the network directly, and a screen rebuild just reads the same data again.
Interviewer: How does the answer appear word by word? SSE, WebSocket, or polling? Why?
Candidate: SSE, because the answer only flows one way, from server to client.
Candidate: It runs over plain HTTP, so it reconnects easily and works with our existing auth.
Candidate: WebSocket is better when both sides talk a lot, like voice mode later.
Candidate: Polling wastes requests and feels slow.
Interviewer: What does one event look like? Show me the format.
Candidate: Each event has an id, a type and the data.
